points: Mass-participation sporting events: organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time.
Usual aim: personal challenge, health or charity, rather than winning.
Types: city marathons, fun runs, parkrun, cycling sportives, open-water swims, obstacle and colour runs and triathlons.
Dublin Marathon: held in Dublin each year.
Women's Mini Marathon: a women's mass-participation event in Dublin.
parkrun: a free, weekly, timed 5 km event held on Saturday mornings.
Great Limerick Run: a mass-participation running event in Limerick.
Health and fitness awareness, promoted nationally.
Charity fundraising and personal challenge goals, such as events people want to complete at least once in their lives.
Social media, apps and wearable trackers make training and sharing results easy.
Inclusive formats: walk, jog or run options, shorter distances, women-only events and free weekly events.
Sponsorship and professional event organisers who market events widely.
Running and cycling clubs, couch-to-5k style programmes and workplace challenges.
Entry fees: income for the organiser and for charities.
Title and partner sponsorship: brands gain exposure to thousands of participants and spectators.
Merchandise and event products: branded T-shirts, medals and photographs; the organiser and the event brand benefit from sales.
Retail: running shoes, clothing, watches, trackers and nutrition products bought for training; sports retailers benefit.
Services: coaching, training plans and apps, physiotherapy, sports massage and timing companies; these providers benefit.
Local economy: hotels, restaurants, pubs, shops and transport are busy on event weekends with visitors from outside the area; local businesses benefit.
Media and advertising: live and online coverage carries sponsors' brands to viewers beyond the start line; broadcasters and advertisers benefit.
Charities: raise large sums through participants' fundraising.
Enterprise: new businesses are set up to organise events, sell event photography, provide timing chips or run training groups; their founders benefit.
Health: participants gain fitness and wellbeing.
Goal-setting: a fixed event date gives participants a training target.
Community spirit: people train, cheer and volunteer together.
Inclusivity: events welcome people of mixed ability.
Charity income: money is raised for good causes.
Road closures and disruption to residents.
Policing and stewarding costs that must be met.
Litter and environmental impact.
Rising entry fees that exclude lower-income groups.
Injury risk for participants who are unprepared.
Events dominated by commercial interests rather than by participants.

keyTerms.definition: An organised event in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for personal challenge, health or charity rather than to win.
A mass-participation cycling event, usually on open roads, for riders of mixed ability.
A swimming event held in natural open water, such as a lake or the sea.
A mass-participation run with physical obstacles set along the route.
The organised supervision of an event by trained staff or volunteers to manage crowds and safety.
The amount each participant pays to take part in an event.
A device worn on the body that records activity, such as steps, heart rate and distance.
A structured training plan that takes a beginner from little or no running to running 5 km.
Raising money for a good cause, often through sponsored participation in an event.
An activity or event organised by an employer to encourage staff to take part in sport.
Branded products, such as T-shirts, medals and photographs, sold to participants and spectators.

questions.prompt: Examine the growth of mass-participation sporting events and the opportunities for business and enterprise they provide.
questions.model: Mass-participation events have grown because health and fitness awareness is promoted nationally, and because charity fundraising and personal challenge goals give people a reason to enter. Social media, apps and wearable trackers make training and sharing results easy, while inclusive formats such as walk, jog or run options, shorter distances and women-only events widen the range of people who take part. Running and cycling clubs, couch-to-5k programmes and workplace challenges bring newcomers in, and sponsorship and professional event organisers market events widely. This growth creates business opportunities. Entry fees bring income to the organiser and to charities, and title and partner sponsorship gives brands exposure to thousands of participants and spectators. Branded T-shirts, medals and photographs give income to the organiser and the event brand. Retailers sell running shoes, clothing, watches, trackers and nutrition products bought for training, and services such as coaching, training plans, physiotherapy, sports massage and timing companies serve participants. Local hotels, restaurants, pubs, shops and transport are busy on event weekends with visitors from outside the area. Media coverage carries sponsors' brands to viewers, and new enterprises can organise events, sell event photography, provide timing chips or run training groups. The Dublin Marathon, the Women's Mini Marathon, parkrun and the Great Limerick Run each illustrate these opportunities. The growth also brings costs, such as road closures and litter, and rising entry fees can exclude lower-income groups.

questions.prompt: Define mass-participation sporting events, give two examples and outline two opportunities they provide for businesses.
questions.model: Mass-participation sporting events are organised events in which large numbers of people of mixed ability take part at the same time, usually for personal challenge, health or charity rather than to win. Two examples are the Dublin Marathon and parkrun. Two opportunities for businesses are: first, merchandise, as branded T-shirts, medals and photographs are sold to participants, giving income to the organiser and the event brand; second, retail, as runners buy running shoes, clothing, watches and trackers for training, giving income to sports retailers.
